response.consequence: With credential sync enabled, a refresh overwrites the stored refresh_token with the string "refresh_token" and the expiry becomes NaN. The next refresh then fails, so users' Zoom connections and the other synced apps break and need re-authorization.
response.explanation: In minimumTokenResponseSchema, `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are ordinary computed keys. Zod schema instances don't override toString, so both evaluate to "[object Object]". The second entry overwrites the first, which leaves the schema as { access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown optional }. These are not wildcard keys, and the "any numeric property is the expiry" intent is not implemented. The hypothesis expected a required "ZodString" key and a parse failure, but that is not what happens. Any response with an access_token parses successfully. Zod's default object mode then strips every other field, including expires_in, expiry_date and the real refresh_token. parseRefreshTokenResponse then sets refresh_token to the literal "refresh_token" on the stripped data. Zoom's caller (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:111-124) takes data.refresh_token and data.expires_in from the result. It stores the placeholder as the refresh token and computes expiry_date as Math.round(Date.now() + undefined*1000), which is NaN. I did not read the Google, Office365 or Salesforce callers.
response.title: Computed schema keys collapse to "[object Object]", so the token response is stripped and the placeholder refresh_token is saved

response.explanation: The changes are import path updates, new env example entries and one new constant. The imported modules exist under _utils/oauth and are used. No schema or stored data changes.
response.title: No persistence defect found

response.consequence: With credential sync enabled, token refresh fails for every caller of parseRefreshTokenResponse (zoom and office365 calendar), so the sync feature does not work.
response.explanation: The schema keys are `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. These evaluate at module load to a fixed literal string such as "[object Object]". They are not wildcard keys. The schema therefore requires a property with that literal name to be a number, and no real token response has one. In credential-sync mode (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT set), every response from the sync endpoint fails safeParse, so parseRefreshTokenResponse throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The default z.object also strips unknown keys, so the expiry field would be dropped even if validation passed. The webhook handler's secret check is not bypassable, because APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED requires CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET to be set.
response.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys from z.string().toString(), so it can never validate a real response

response.consequence: Timing comparison of the secret is only a minor risk over a network. Malformed webhook payloads produce 500 responses with unhandled exceptions rather than clean 400s.
response.explanation: The auth bypass in the hypothesis does not happen. APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is defined in packages/lib/constants.ts:103 as CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY. The handler returns 403 at line 19 unless both are non-empty. So an unset secret cannot match a missing header, and the `|| ""` key fallback at line 56 cannot be reached with an empty key. Two weaker defects remain. (1) The secret check at lines 24-27 uses `!==`, which is not constant-time, so response timing can leak the secret. (2) `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` (line 30) and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (lines 55-57) are not wrapped in try/catch. A malformed body, a bad ciphertext or invalid JSON throws, and the caller gets a 500 instead of a 400.
response.title: Webhook secret compared with !== (not constant-time); parse and decrypt errors are unhandled

response.consequence: A non-admin team member can install or overwrite team-level app credentials, such as calendar or video integrations, which the code intends to restrict to team admins. Malformed state values also cause a 500 instead of a 4xx.
response.explanation: createOAuthAppCredential takes teamId from the unsigned JSON in req.query.state. When state.teamId is set, it only checks that the session user is an accepted member of that team (lines 30-45). It then creates a team credential and returns (lines 47-56). throwIfNotHaveAdminAccessToTeam is called only after that branch, at line 59. By then state.teamId is falsy, so the call is always passed null and returns immediately. The admin check is therefore dead code. A plain team member can set state={"teamId":N} on the OAuth callback and create a credential for that team. The state has no signature, nonce or session binding, so it can be forged or replayed (decodeOAuthState.ts, encodeOAuthState.ts). JSON.parse in decodeOAuthState is unguarded, so malformed state throws and gives a 500.
response.title: Team credential created for any accepted member using unsigned, client-controlled state.teamId; admin check is never applied

response.consequence: With APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and a sync endpoint configured, Google Calendar token refresh always fails. The failure is swallowed and the expired access token keeps being used, so calendar calls fail. Error responses from the sync endpoint are not detected.
response.explanation: When credential sharing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the fetch Response from the sync endpoint. It does not check the status and does not parse the body. The Google caller reads `res?.data`, which is an axios/googleapis shape. A fetch Response has no `.data`, so `token` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The surrounding catch only handles the `invalid_grant` message. Any other error returns `myGoogleAuth` silently, so the token is never refreshed from the sync endpoint and the credential is not updated. The Google caller also passes `googleCredentials`, not the refreshed response, to parseRefreshTokenResponse. A successful sync-endpoint response would therefore never be validated or persisted. The two branches of refreshOAuthTokens return different shapes. The refresh-function branch returns googleapis `res`, which has `.data`. The sync branch returns a fetch Response, which needs `.json()`. Because the sync branch does not check `response.ok`, a non-2xx response from the sync endpoint is also handed to callers as if it were a token response. The Office365 caller uses `handleErrorsJson(response)`, which works with a Response, so it is not affected by the shape mismatch.
response.title: Sync-endpoint branch returns a raw fetch Response, which Google's refresh path reads as axios-style `.data`

response.explanation: The change only adds four environment variable names to turbo.json globalEnv. The JSON stays valid and the entries are not duplicated. Adding them only makes the cache hash depend on these variables, which is the intended effect.
response.title: No defect in added globalEnv entries

response.consequence: After the first successful token refresh, the user's Google Calendar credential is corrupted in the database. Every later Google Calendar operation for that credential throws a parse error until the user reconnects.
response.explanation: The change replaced `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`, which returned the parsed credential, with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)`. That helper returns the zod `safeParse` result, `{ success, data }`. The result is assigned to `key` and written with `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The stored credential key becomes `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. The next read through `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` at the top of `googleAuth` fails because `access_token`, `refresh_token` and the other fields are missing at the top level.

other_findings.consequence: Constructing `SalesforceCalendarService` rejects on every call, so Salesforce integration is broken. If the missing import were added, the connection would still use the expired token.
other_findings.explanation: The new refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update` at line 96. The grep for `prisma` in this file finds only that line, so there is no import of `@calcom/prisma`. Running `getClient` therefore throws a ReferenceError. Separately, the refreshed token is never used. The `jsforce.Connection` at line 106 is still built with `credentialKey.access_token`, the old token, instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.
other_findings.title: Salesforce getClient uses prisma without importing it and builds the connection with the stale access token

If CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset and the header is absent, undefined === undefined passes, so anyone can write credentials. The comparison is also not constant-time.
